audio_caption: The clip begins with a male speaker announcing, "And we're back now," setting a conversational tone. He introduces Congressman Ron Paul and mentions his location in Fairbanks, Alaska. The speaker notes the presence of "24 delegates up there for grabs on Tuesday," and then asks the Congressman, "Where do you think that you can win on Tuesday night?".

The audio clip features a male speaker discussing his "measurement of winning", defined as winning the majority of delegates. He mentions several states where he believes he may win, including Alaska, Idaho, and North Dakota. The speaker sounds confident and uses a conversational tone. Subsequently, another male speaker begins to speak, asking a serious question with respect. The conversation unfolds against a quiet background.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker being asked if he is "in this to the end," and whether he thinks he could win the nomination. The speaker begins to answer the question in a calm tone, emphasizing that he doesn't see why there needs to be an "either or" situation. He further elaborates that winning is the best way to promote a cause, referring to his past successes in Congress and arguing that promoting the idea of a strict constitutional view and sound money through his elections was very beneficial to that cause. He concludes that it doesn't bother him.

A male speaker addresses a question of belief, stating "do I believe I can win? Yes, do I believe the chances are slim? Yes," before acknowledging uncertainty due to external factors. He speaks in a conversational tone, indicating he doesn't believe the situation is an either/or issue.

A male speaker begins, stating that he takes "from what you're just telling me this morning" that the purpose is "to make a point." He elaborates, mentioning the libertarian point of view and how the intention is to strengthen libertarians rather than focusing on winning a nomination. The speaker has a formal tone.
The audio clip begins with a male speaker stating, "Well, no." He then explains that he said something different, specifying that "both, both are mutual." His tone is conversational.

A male speaker expresses frustration at the focus on gaining power in politics, noting the lack of difference between parties in foreign and monetary policy and concern for personal liberties. His tone is impassioned and somewhat exasperated. He discusses the confusion of encountering someone who seems to care about issues more than power, but acknowledges the need for influence and political action to effect change, ending by mentioning the determination of his supporters to win.

The audio clip starts with a male interviewer asking a question about Rick Santorum saying the interviewee was "in cahoots with Mitt Romney". The speaking tone is conversational and inquisitive. Then, the clip abruptly ends.

The clip features a male speaker addressing another male speaker, who responds in a conversational tone. The first man mentions that some have suggested the second is trying to "create a situation where Romney might ask your son, Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, to be his running mate." The second man replies dismissively, saying it "sounds like he's trying to concoct a conspiracy," and stating he believes it's created. He suggests the media has "fed on that" and concludes by characterizing his opponent's attacks as "silly."

The audio clip opens with someone talking about a prominent figure apologizing for calling a young woman a "prostitute" after her testimony on government healthcare plans. The speaker has a conversational, inquiring tone.  The speaker then asks about the apology and how social issues play into the campaign. The tone of the speaker appears to be seeking some sort of answer, or judgement.

The clip features a single male speaker with a slightly assertive tone, discussing the need for an apology from someone who used crude language and criticizing them for being insincere. He suggests the person only apologized due to advertisers withdrawing support, impacting their "bottom line." The speaker then transitions to discussing birth control, stating someone doesn't believe people should use it and contrasting this with his own support as an OB doctor. The speaker indicates the discussion is shifting to a different topic.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker discussing the philosophical and political importance of government mandates regarding insurance coverage. He questions whether the government has the right to dictate what insurance companies provide, specifically mentioning free birth control pills and the perceived unfairness of individuals paying for services they may not use or morally object to. The speaker's tone is inquisitive and critical, with a slightly agitated delivery. His argument focuses on the principle of choice in insurance coverage, using OB care as an example.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker critiquing a situation, labeling it as a "total destruction of the marketplace", while discussing mandates related to Obama and Republicans. He questions why people who strongly believe in right-to-life should have to pay for abortion, while also criticizing Santorum's past funding of Planned Parenthood. His tone is critical and disapproving, ending by calling someone a "fake conservative". The clip concludes with another male voice simply saying "Alright."

The audio begins with a male speaker greeting someone, stating "it's always good to talk to you" and thanking them for waking up early, spoken in a conversational tone. The speech then ends and there are no other audible sounds.
